title: ACCA FA - Financial Accounting
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA FA syllabus study guide. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: A private investor who owns shares in a listed company wants to decide whether to buy more shares. Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which user group does this investor belong to?
items.explanation: The Conceptual Framework identifies existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors as the primary users of general purpose financial statements. Management and tax authorities may also use them, but they are not the primary audience.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: Which qualitative characteristic of useful financial information is described as information that is capable of making a difference in the decisions made by users?
items.explanation: Relevance means the information is capable of making a difference to decisions through its predictive value, its confirmatory value, or both. Faithful representation concerns completeness, neutrality and freedom from error rather than decision impact.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: An entity reports a profit for the year but will not receive the related cash until the following year. Which underlying assumption of financial reporting justifies recognising the income now?
items.explanation: Under the accrual basis, income and expenses are recognised when the underlying transaction occurs rather than when cash is received or paid. Going concern assumes the entity will continue in operation for the foreseeable future and does not itself time the recognition.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: The directors of an entity believe it will continue in operation for the foreseeable future with neither the intention nor the need to liquidate. Which underlying assumption are they applying?
items.explanation: The going concern assumption presumes the entity will continue in operation for the foreseeable future. If it were not a going concern, assets would be valued on a break-up basis instead of at historical cost.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: Which body is responsible for issuing International Financial Reporting Standards that are used by entities preparing financial statements under IFRS?
items.explanation: The International Accounting Standards Board, the standard-setting body of the IFRS Foundation, issues IFRS and the IFRS for SMEs Standard. Auditors apply the standards and tax authorities are separate from the standard-setting process.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: An entity sells goods with a right of return and the buyer is very likely to return them. Which concept requires the economic substance of the arrangement to be reflected rather than its legal form?
items.explanation: Faithful representation requires that transactions are accounted for according to their economic substance, not merely their legal form. This is why a sale with an almost certain return may not be recognised as revenue.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: Which statement best describes the objective of general purpose financial statements according to the IASB Conceptual Framework?
options: To guarantee that the entity will remain profitable
To provide information mainly to the government for economic planning
To provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors
To report the entity's taxable profit to the tax authority
items.explanation: The objective is to provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to primary users in making decisions about providing resources to the entity. It does not guarantee profitability nor serve governments alone.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.domain: The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting
items.stem: Two entities are identical except that one uses the reducing-balance method for depreciation while the other uses the straight-line method. Which enhancing qualitative characteristic is improved when an entity applies its accounting policies consistently from year to year?
items.explanation: Comparability is enhanced when an entity applies its accounting policies consistently over time, allowing users to identify trends. Consistency is one of the ingredients of comparability, while timeliness and verifiability concern other aspects of usefulness.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - The Context and Purpose of Financial Reporting

items.stem: A business buys office equipment for cash of 5,000. Which double entry correctly records this transaction?
options: Debit office equipment 5,000 and credit cash 5,000
Debit cash 5,000 and credit office equipment 5,000
Debit office equipment 5,000 and credit capital 5,000
items.explanation: Buying an asset for cash increases the asset office equipment, which is debited, and decreases the asset cash, which is credited. Crediting capital would be wrong because no new capital was introduced by the owner.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A trader makes a credit sale of goods for 400. Which book of prime entry should the transaction first be recorded in?
items.explanation: Credit sales are first recorded in the sales day book, from which totals are posted to the ledger. Cash sales go to the cash book and credit purchases to the purchase day book.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity pays an annual insurance premium of 2,400 on 1 October for the twelve months to the following 30 September. Its year end is 31 December. Which amount should be charged as insurance expense for the year?
items.explanation: Only three months of cover, from 1 October to 31 December, relates to the current year, so the expense is 2,400 multiplied by three twelfths, which is 600. The remaining 1,800 is a prepayment carried forward.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity's electricity bill for the three months to 31 March, its year end, is received in April and amounts to 900. No entry has yet been made. Which adjustment is required at the year end?
options: Debit prepayments and credit electricity expense 900
Debit electricity expense and credit cash 900
Debit accruals and credit electricity expense 900
Debit electricity expense and credit accruals 900
items.explanation: The expense relates to the current year but the invoice arrives later, so an accrual is raised by debiting the expense and crediting accruals. Crediting cash would be wrong because no cash has yet been paid.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A machine costing 12,000 has an estimated residual value of 2,000 and a useful life of five years. Using the straight-line method, which amount is the annual depreciation charge?
items.explanation: Depreciation is the depreciable amount of 12,000 minus 2,000, which is 10,000, divided by five years, giving 2,000 per year. Using the full cost without deducting residual value would give 2,400.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A vehicle costs 10,000 and is depreciated at 20 percent per year on the reducing-balance basis. Which amount is the depreciation charge in the second year?
items.explanation: In the first year depreciation is 20 percent of 10,000, or 2,000, leaving a carrying amount of 8,000. The second-year charge is 20 percent of 8,000, which is 1,600. Charging 2,000 again would be the straight-line treatment.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: At the year end a business has inventory that cost 9,000. Its net realisable value is estimated at 8,200. At which amount should the inventory be stated in the financial statements?
items.explanation: Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Because the net realisable value of 8,200 is below the cost of 9,000, the inventory is written down to 8,200.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: During the year a business sells goods to a customer on credit for 500. The customer returns faulty goods that were sold for 200. Which entry records the return in the seller's books?
options: Debit receivables and credit sales returns 200
Debit sales returns and credit receivables 200
items.explanation: A sales return reduces the amount owed by the customer, so receivables is credited, and it is recorded in a sales returns account that is debited. Debiting sales would confuse the main sales account with returns.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A business uses the allowance method for receivables and decides that a specific debt of 300 is irrecoverable. Which entry writes the debt off?
options: Debit irrecoverable debts expense and credit receivables 300
Debit receivables and credit irrecoverable debts expense 300
Debit allowance for receivables and credit cash 300
items.explanation: Writing off a debt removes it from receivables by crediting that account and recognises the expense by debiting irrecoverable debts expense. Cash is not involved because the amount will not be collected.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: At the year end receivables total 40,000 and an allowance for receivables of 2 percent is to be created for the first time. Which amount is charged to the statement of profit or loss?
items.explanation: The allowance is 2 percent of 40,000, which is 800. Because no allowance existed before, the full 800 is charged to profit or loss in the current year.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity's bank statement shows a balance of 5,000 while the cash book shows 4,700. Cheques drawn by the entity and not yet presented at the bank total 500. What is the most likely explanation for the difference?
options: The entity has recorded a receipt twice
There is an irrecoverable debt of 500
Cheques drawn by the entity have not yet been presented at the bank
The bank has overcharged the entity by 500
items.explanation: Cheques written by the entity reduce the cash book when issued but reduce the bank balance only when presented. Unpresented cheques of 500 explain the bank statement being higher than the cash book.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A business registered for sales tax makes a standard-rated credit sale. Which account is credited with the sales tax element of the sale?
items.explanation: Sales tax charged on sales is not part of revenue, so the net amount is credited to sales and the tax element is credited to the sales tax payable account. Sales tax recoverable is used for tax paid on purchases.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity records a credit purchase of goods for 3,000 from a supplier on normal credit terms. Which entry is correct?
items.explanation: A credit purchase increases purchases, an expense that is debited, and increases payables, a liability that is credited. Cash is not involved because the purchase is made on credit.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A business has an allowance for doubtful debts of 1,000 at the start of the year and 1,500 at the end of the year. Which amount is charged to the statement of profit or loss as an increase in the allowance?
items.explanation: The increase in the allowance is 1,500 minus 1,000, which is 500, and this amount is charged to profit or loss. The full closing allowance of 1,500 is only charged when no opening allowance exists.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A trader's cash book shows a debit balance of 2,000. A bank reconciliation reveals bank charges of 100 not yet entered in the cash book. Which amount is the corrected cash book balance?
items.explanation: Bank charges reduce the bank balance and have not been recorded, so the cash book balance of 2,000 is reduced by 100 to give 1,900. The charges are entered as a credit in the cash book.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity receives an invoice from a supplier for goods of 4,000 less a 5 percent trade discount. Which amount is recorded for the purchase net of the trade discount?
items.explanation: A trade discount is deducted before the invoice is entered, so the recorded amount is 4,000 less 5 percent, which is 4,000 minus 200, giving 3,800. Settlement discounts depend on prompt payment and are treated differently.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A business takes out a bank loan of 10,000 and immediately uses the money to buy machinery. Which pair of entries correctly records the receipt of the loan and the purchase?
options: Debit bank and credit loan, then debit machinery and credit bank
Debit machinery and credit loan only
Debit loan and credit bank, then debit bank and credit machinery
Debit capital and credit loan only
items.explanation: Receiving the loan increases the bank asset, which is debited, and increases the loan liability, which is credited. Buying machinery then debits the machinery asset and credits bank, so the two steps are recorded separately.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: An entity's rent account is debited with amounts paid of 6,000. The closing accrual for rent is 500 and the opening accrual brought forward was 300. Which amount is the rent expense for the year?
items.explanation: Rent expense equals the amount paid of 6,000 plus the closing accrual of 500 less the opening accrual of 300, which gives 6,200. Adding the opening accrual instead of deducting it would double count it.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Recording Transactions and Events

items.stem: A trial balance fails to agree and the difference of 100 is placed in a suspense account. Which type of error would cause the trial balance to be out of balance by that amount?
options: A complete omission of a transaction
A compensating error of equal amounts
A transposition of a single account balance
items.explanation: A one-sided entry affects only one account and unbalances the trial balance by the amount involved. Complete omission, compensating errors and many transpositions have no net effect on the trial balance totals.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A business purchases a delivery van but records the cost in the motor expenses account. Which type of error has occurred?
items.explanation: Recording a capital item as revenue expenditure is an error of principle because it breaks the rule that expenditure should be classified correctly. An error of commission is a posting to the wrong account of the same type.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A supplier's invoice for 250 is entered in the books as 520 and posted to the correct accounts. Which type of error is this?
items.explanation: When an incorrect figure is entered in a book of prime entry, the error is one of original entry. Because both accounts receive the same wrong figure, the trial balance still agrees.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: An entity debits an account with 500 where a credit of 500 was intended, and the other side of the entry is correct. How is this error corrected?
options: By ignoring it because the trial balance agrees
By debiting the account and crediting the suspense account with 1,000
By crediting the account with 500 only
By debiting the account with another 500 only
items.explanation: The account wrongly contains a debit of 500 that should be a credit, so the debit must be removed and the correct credit entered, a net correction of 1,000 on that side. The suspense account is credited to restore the balance.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A credit sale of 900 to A. Bell is entered in B. Bell's account. The trial balance still agrees. Which type of error has occurred?
items.explanation: Posting to the wrong but similarly named account is an error of commission. Because both entries were made, the trial balance is unaffected, but the individual receivables accounts are wrong.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A purchase of office stationery for 60 was entered in the stationery account as 600 and in the payables account as 60. Which correction is needed in the stationery account?
items.explanation: The stationery account is overstated by 540, so it must be credited with 540 to reduce it to the correct 60. The payables account is already correct, so no correction is needed there.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: The sales ledger control account shows a debit balance of 15,000, but the list of individual receivable balances totals 14,700. A credit sale of 300 was completely omitted from the receivables ledger. Which adjustment corrects the list of balances?
options: Add 300 to the list of balances
Deduct 300 from the list of balances
items.explanation: The control account total of 15,000 is correct because the transaction was recorded there. Because the individual ledger omitted the 300 sale, the list of balances must be increased by 300 to reconcile with the control account.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A bank reconciliation statement starts with the balance per the bank statement and adjusts for items such as unpresented cheques and lodgements not yet credited. Which item is added back to the bank statement balance?
options: Standing order payments made by the bank
Deposits credited by the entity but not yet showing on the bank statement
Bank charges not recorded in the cash book
items.explanation: Lodgements not yet credited by the bank mean the bank statement is lower than the true balance, so they are added back. Unpresented cheques, bank charges and standing orders make the statement balance higher and are deducted.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: A trial balance is prepared and the total debits exceed the total credits by 210, a difference that is exactly divisible by nine. Which error is most likely?
options: A complete omission of a transaction
items.explanation: A transposition error, in which two digits are reversed, produces a difference that is exactly divisible by nine. Complete omissions, errors of principle and compensating errors do not unbalance the trial balance.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: An entertainment expense of 45 has been completely omitted from the accounting records. What is the effect of this omission on the trial balance?
options: The trial balance still agrees because both sides are omitted
items.explanation: Complete omission means neither the debit nor the credit was recorded, so the trial balance totals remain equal. Only a one-sided entry would cause the trial balance to disagree.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing a Trial Balance

items.stem: Which of the following is classified as a non-current liability in a statement of financial position?
options: A bank loan repayable in five years
items.explanation: Non-current liabilities are obligations due more than twelve months after the reporting date, so a five-year bank loan qualifies. Trade payables are current liabilities, while inventory and cash are current assets.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity has revenue of 200,000, opening inventory of 15,000, purchases of 120,000 and closing inventory of 20,000. Which amount is the cost of sales?
items.explanation: Cost of sales equals opening inventory plus purchases less closing inventory, so 15,000 plus 120,000 minus 20,000 equals 115,000. Omitting opening inventory would understate the figure.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: Using revenue of 200,000 and a cost of sales of 115,000, which amount is the gross profit for the year?
items.explanation: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of sales, so 200,000 minus 115,000 equals 85,000. Adding the two figures would give the meaningless total of 315,000, which ignores the meaning of gross profit.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity has gross profit of 85,000 and expenses for administration, selling and distribution of 30,000. Which amount is the operating profit?
items.explanation: Operating profit is gross profit less operating expenses, so 85,000 minus 30,000 equals 55,000. Interest and tax are deducted after this figure to reach profit for the year.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: At the start of the year an entity's capital is 50,000. During the year it earns a profit of 12,000 and the owner withdraws 5,000 in drawings. Which amount is the closing capital?
items.explanation: Closing capital equals opening capital of 50,000 plus profit of 12,000 less drawings of 5,000, which gives 57,000. Ignoring drawings would overstate capital at 62,000.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity buys a machine for 30,000 on the last day of its financial year and pays cash. How should this be shown in the statement of financial position prepared at that date?
options: As a non-current asset with a corresponding reduction in cash
As an expense in the statement of profit or loss
items.explanation: The machine is a non-current asset because it will be used in the business over more than one period, and cash falls by the same amount. It is not expensed because the asset still provides future benefit.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity reports retained earnings of 40,000 at the start of the year and profit for the year of 25,000. It declares dividends of 10,000. Which amount is the closing retained earnings?
items.explanation: Closing retained earnings equals opening retained earnings of 40,000 plus profit of 25,000 less dividends of 10,000, giving 55,000. Forgetting to deduct the dividends would overstate the reserve at 65,000.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: After the reporting date but before the financial statements are authorised for issue, a customer with a large balance owing is declared bankrupt and this confirms a condition that existed at the reporting date. How should the entity treat this event?
options: Do nothing because it happened after the year end
Only disclose it in the notes without adjusting
Reverse the sale as revenue of the following year
Adjust the financial statements to write down the receivable
items.explanation: This is an adjusting event because it provides evidence of a condition that existed at the reporting date, so the receivable and profit are adjusted. Non-adjusting events are only disclosed in the notes.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: Which financial statement reports the assets, liabilities and equity of an entity at a specific point in time?
options: The statement of profit or loss
The statement of changes in equity
items.explanation: The statement of financial position presents assets, liabilities and equity as at the reporting date, so it is a snapshot at a point in time. The other statements cover a period of time.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity has non-current assets of 80,000, current assets of 30,000, current liabilities of 20,000 and non-current liabilities of 25,000. Which amount is total equity?
items.explanation: Equity is total assets less total liabilities. Total assets are 80,000 plus 30,000, which is 110,000, and total liabilities are 20,000 plus 25,000, which is 45,000, giving equity of 65,000.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity's revenue for the year is 500,000 and its cost of sales is 300,000. Which amount is the gross profit margin expressed as a percentage of revenue?
items.explanation: Gross profit is 500,000 minus 300,000, which is 200,000. Dividing 200,000 by revenue of 500,000 gives 40 percent. The 60 percent figure is cost of sales as a share of revenue, not the gross margin.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: Which item would be presented under current assets in a statement of financial position?
options: A building used as the entity's head office
A loan repayable in ten years
Share capital issued by the entity
Inventories expected to be sold within twelve months
items.explanation: Inventories are current assets because they are expected to be realised within the normal operating cycle or twelve months. A head office building is non-current and share capital is equity, not an asset.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: An entity's statement of profit or loss shows profit before tax of 60,000. The tax charge is 15,000 and an interim dividend of 5,000 has been paid. Which amount is the profit for the year?
items.explanation: Profit for the year is profit before tax of 60,000 less the tax charge of 15,000, which is 45,000. Dividends are not an expense and are deducted in the statement of changes in equity.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements

items.stem: A sole trader's statement of financial position shows net assets of 90,000. Which statement about the relationship between net assets and capital is correct?
options: Capital equals net assets because assets less liabilities equals the owner's interest
Capital is always twice the net assets
Net assets exclude the owner's drawings from the capital figure
items.explanation: By the accounting equation, assets less liabilities equals capital, so net assets of 90,000 equal the owner's capital. Drawings have already been reflected in the capital figure, and net assets include both non-current and current items.
items.reference: ACCA FA Syllabus Study Guide - Preparing Basic Financial Statements
